title: Data is Your Differentiator: Building Secure and Tailored AI Systems — Mani Khanuja, AWS

summary: Mani Khanuja frames her talk around the idea that data is the critical differentiator for enterprise generative AI. While data transformation and loading remain important, the new challenge is how data interacts with technology, people, and applications, and breaking down data silos. She illustrates this with three use cases: a travel agent requiring customer profiles, company travel policies, and PII protection; an internal contextual chatbot requiring company data with proper access controls; and marketing applications with distinct data needs. She deep-dives into the travel agent scenario, noting data is needed at every step—prompts, context, and model fine-tuning. Amazon Bedrock is presented as the solution stack, offering model choice, Bedrock Data Automation (BDA) for custom data pipelines via a single API, model customization and evaluation, Knowledge Bases for rapid RAG application development, and Guardrails for responsible AI. For a contextual chatbot, BDA processes multimedia content including financial documents with charts and graphs. Knowledge Bases provide native BDA integration, chunking strategies, embeddings model selection, vector store choice, incremental updates, a Retrieve API supporting hybrid search, and a Retrieve and Generate API with built-in reranking and query decomposition. Guardrails enable PII filtering, custom policies, response grounding, and user interaction logging. In the closing segment, Khanuja returns to the coconuts metaphor to deliver best practices applicable to RAG and other generative AI applications. She emphasizes that chunking strategy is important but only one step; optimization—including reranking, hybrid search, query reformulation, and decomposition—is also essential. She identifies accuracy, cost, and latency as the three pillars of generative AI performance, recommending semantic caching to avoid redundant foundation model invocations. Observability—logging user queries, retrieval hits, and model responses—is declared critical; she advises never going to production or even piloting without it. Evaluation follows, including context relevance checks for RAG before invoking the model, plus use-case-specific metrics such as summarization metrics. When issues arise, teams must update stale data or strategies, then retest using automated test suites to reduce production errors. She closes by tying the coconut metaphor to scaling: after cracking and decorating coconuts, organizations can bear the fruits of success in production.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: Data is the foundational differentiator for generative AI, and data requirements differ by use case and business requirements.
Amazon Bedrock provides an integrated suite: Bedrock Data Automation, Knowledge Bases, Guardrails, model customization, and model evaluation.

Bedrock Knowledge Bases offer chunking strategies, vectorization, vector store choice, incremental updates, Retrieve API with hybrid search, and Retrieve and Generate API with reranking and query decomposition.
Bedrock Guardrails provide PII filtering, custom policies, response grounding to reduce hallucinations, and user interaction logging for responsible AI.
Optimization across accuracy, cost, and latency is essential—techniques include semantic caching, reranking, hybrid search, query reformulation, and decomposition.
Observability is critical: log user queries, retrieval hits, and model responses; do not pilot or go to production without it.
Evaluate applications before invoking the model—check context relevance for RAG and use use-case-specific metrics such as summarization metrics.
After updates to data or strategy, run automated test suites to reduce production errors and increase application quality.
The animated dancing coconuts, generated by Amazon Nova models, serve as a recurring metaphor: crack the coconut to scale, decorate it for production, and bear the fruits of success.
Understand how data requirements vary across generative AI use cases such as travel agents, chatbots, and marketing.

sections.title: Opening and Coconuts Intro
sections.summary: Khanuja opens with animated dancing coconuts generated by Amazon Nova models, setting a light tone before transitioning to the core topic of data as a differentiator.

sections.title: Data as the Foundation for Generative AI
sections.summary: Establishes that generative AI adds significant business value if done right, but the foundation must be deep—and that foundation is data representing the company, brand, and organization. Data requirements for generative AI are different from traditional ML and require special treatment. The key challenge is how data interacts with technology and people, and breaking down data silos.

sections.title: Use Case Examples and Varying Data Requirements
sections.summary: Presents three use cases: a travel agent (needs customer profiles, company travel policies, PII protection), an internal contextual chatbot for employee productivity (needs company data with proper access controls and integrations like Slack), and marketing (distinct data needs). Concludes that data requirements differ per use case, then deep-dives into the travel agent showing data needed at every step: prompts, context from data sources, and fine-tuning data.

sections.title: Amazon Bedrock Overview
sections.summary: Introduces Amazon Bedrock as the solution, providing model choice, Bedrock Data Automation for custom data pipelines, model customizations, model evaluation, Knowledge Bases for rapid RAG development, and Guardrails for responsible AI. Emphasizes all applications must be built securely and privately with safety guardrails.

sections.title: Building a RAG Chatbot with BDA and Knowledge Bases
sections.summary: Walks through building a contextual chatbot: BDA for data processing (including financial documents with charts), Knowledge Bases for chunking strategies (hierarchical, semantic, custom), embeddings model selection, vector store choice, incremental updates, Retrieve API with hybrid search, and Retrieve and Generate API with built-in reranking and query decomposition—all configurable via parameters without custom code.

sections.title: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails for Responsible AI
sections.summary: Covers Guardrails features for responsible AI: PII filtering, blocking undesirable keywords, custom policies, response grounding to reduce hallucinations, and user interaction logging to identify patterns. Notes native integration with Knowledge Bases and teases the return of the coconuts motif.

sections.title: Best Practices, Optimization, and the Coconuts Metaphor
sections.summary: Returns to the coconuts metaphor to deliver best practices for RAG and other generative AI applications. Covers chunking strategy as one important step, then optimization (reranking, hybrid search, query reformulation, decomposition) across three pillars: accuracy, cost, and latency. Recommends semantic caching to avoid redundant model invocations. Emphasizes observability—logging queries, retrieval hits, and model responses—as critical before piloting or production. Discusses evaluation including context relevance for RAG and use-case-specific metrics. Stresses updating stale data or strategies, then retesting with automated test suites to reduce production errors. Closes with the coconut metaphor: crack the coconut to scale, decorate it for production, and bear the fruits of success.

demonstrations: Animated dancing coconuts generated by Amazon Nova models shown at the start of the talk and revisited as a metaphor for production readiness.
limitations: Limited presentation time prevented covering every Guardrails feature in detail.
